title: MKD2World: A Typed Spatial Markdown World Model for Web Agents

paper.title: MKD2World: A Typed Spatial Markdown World Model for Web Agents
paper.abstract:
Abstract Graphical user interface (GUI) agents can improve decision-making with world-model foresight,
provided that predicted states accurately reflect post-action interfaces.
Existing state representations fail to jointly capture interface layout, UI semantics, and explicit locations.
We introduce Typed Spatial Markdown (TSM) , a Markdown-style textual state representation for desktop web interfaces.
TSM serializes block-level and atomic-level UI elements according to their spatial relationships,
jointly encoding their types, visual semantics, explicit locations, optional control states, and hierarchical membership.
To train a screenshot-to-TSM renderer, we construct AtomBlock-WebUI , a dataset with precise annotations at both granularities.
By injecting element-type labels into HTML and directly extracting bounding boxes after rendering, we avoid annotation errors caused by post-hoc inference from webpage structures.
Building on TSM, we propose MKD2World , a desktop web world model trained in two stages
for current-state description and action-conditioned next-state prediction.
During inference, the web agent queries MKD2World as needed and performs a “digest” step,
in which it interprets each predicted state and extracts task-relevant evidence for selecting the best action.
Experiments show that MKD2World-9B achieves an EleF1 score of 26.50 on the out-of-domain test set, outperforming GPT-5.6-Sol(14.98) by 11.52 points.
Across Online-Mind2Web tasks, MKD2World-9B improves the success rate of the Qwen3.5-35B web agent from 22.94% to 37.61%,
achieving competitive performance among leading open-source GUI world models. Code is available at https://github.com/OmniAI-Lab-CUHKSZ/MKD2World .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: With the development of vision-language models (VLMs), graphical user interface (GUI) agents have become capable of completing interactive tasks in real-world scenarios ( Cao et al., 2026a ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) . At each decision step, an agent generates an executable action based on the task objective, current interface, and historical information. However, without sufficient understanding of webpage dynamics—including the functions of user interface (UI) controls and the logic of interface transitions—it may generate ineffective actions that increase interaction costs or cause irreversible errors, such as accidentally deleting important data or leaking private information ( Shen et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Action-conditioned world models offer a promising way to anticipate future interface states before execution, helping agents assess whether candidate actions advance the task while reducing risky real interactions ( Mei et al., 2026 ; Gu et al., 2025 ) . Figure 1: Comparing GUI state representations for world models. TSM better balances a complete, structured interface state with low reconstruction cost. The usefulness of such foresight depends on what state a world model predicts . Figure 1 compares representative GUI state representations and highlights the desired trade-off: preserving a complete, structured interface state without incurring the cost of pixel-level reconstruction. We argue that, to distinguish the consequences of candidate actions, a predicted state should preserve a complete yet structured account of the post-action interface, including both the elements that change and the surrounding context needed to interpret those changes—their semantics, locations, control states, and structural relations. At the same time, it should avoid the cost and instability of reconstructing every visual detail of a webpage. Existing GUI world models represent states as free-form descriptions of interface changes, structured interface representations such as the Accessibility Tree (AXTree) and Document Object Model (DOM) ( Zuo et al., 2026 ) , HTML rendered into webpages ( Koh et al., 2026 ) , or images generated directly by image generation models ( Guan et al., 2026 ) . Free-form text concisely conveys major changes but loses layout structure and substantial information from the next interface. Common AXTree and DOM serializations preserve parts of the interface structure, yet often omit explicit element locations and have incomplete visual semantics ( Wu et al., 2023 ) . Other structured textual representations retain some layout and locations, but support limited element types and omit UI control states, complete visual semantics, or interface block structure ( Cao et al., 2026b ) . HTML-rendered images may omit actual images or deviate from the real layout, whereas pure image-generation approaches are costly and often distort fine-grained text ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) . Thus, these representations do not adequately balance preserving a complete, structured interface state with avoiding the burden of full visual reconstruction. This limits the completeness of the interface information available to a world model and, in turn, to downstream agent reasoning. To address this bottleneck, we introduce Typed Spatial Markdown (TSM) , a structured and spatially grounded state representation for desktop Web interfaces. TSM organizes rendered Web UIs into block-level and atomic-level elements according to their spatial relationships. Each entry encodes its type, visual semantics, bounding box, optional control state, and hierarchical membership, jointly capturing what an element is, where it appears, what it conveys, and how it is organized. Markdown provides a readable hierarchical serialization of this structured state. By retaining the interface information needed to compare action-induced changes without reconstructing the full pixel-level interface, TSM provides a compact and directly comparable state space for action-conditioned world modeling and downstream agent reasoning. Learning this state space from screenshots requires reliable UI element types and locations. Existing desktop Web UI datasets often extract them from the DOM or AXTree through rule-based parsing ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Gurbuz et al., 2026 ) . However, HTML structures are highly heterogeneous across webpages: tags and class names are typically tied to page styling and interactions, while role attributes are often incomplete, making unified and reliable semantic annotations difficult to obtain ( Gou et al., 2025 ) . Post-hoc DOM parsing can therefore assign types to visually invisible elements or yield misaligned bounding boxes; visual models may likewise localize elements away from their actual positions ( Fu et al., 2026 ) . To reduce ambiguities introduced by such post-hoc semantic inference, we construct AtomBlock-WebUI . A VLM generates HTML with reference to real webpage layouts and explicitly injects predefined UI element types. After rendering, we directly extract the coordinates of the corresponding typed DOM nodes. This pipeline provides visually aligned type and location supervision for the dual-granularity UI detector in our TSM renderer. Building on TSM and AtomBlock-WebUI, we introduce MKD2World , an action-conditioned desktop Web world model that predicts future TSM states from screenshots and candidate actions. MKD2World first learns to reconstruct the current interface in the TSM state space, and then learns action-conditioned state transitions with transition-aware objectives that emphasize the elements changed by an action. At inference time, it simulates a next TSM state for each candidate action. We further train the GUI agent to understand TSM and design a digest-based inference strategy, through which the agent interprets predicted typed, spatial, and stateful changes to select the action that best advances the user objective. The main contributions of this work are as follows: • Typed Spatial Markdown (TSM). We propose TSM, a structured and spatially grounded Web UI state representation that encodes UI semantics, explicit spatial information, control states, and hierarchical structures, together with a screenshot-to-TSM renderer. • AtomBlock-WebUI Dataset. We construct a 9.7k-scale desktop Web UI annotation dataset using a pre-injected automated annotation pipeline, providing element types and bounding boxes for both block-level and atomic-level UI elements to train the dual-granularity UI detector in the screenshot-to-TSM renderer. • MKD2World: A TSM World Model for Web Agents. We propose MKD2World, an action-conditioned desktop Web world model that predicts future TSM states from screenshots and candidate actions. MKD2World uses a two-stage training scheme with transition-aware objectives, and supports uncertainty-triggered, digest-based action selection by TSM-aware Web agents. • Comprehensive Evaluation and Online Validation. We propose EleF1 to evaluate TSM prediction accuracy, and demonstrate strong out-of-domain prediction and consistent decision-making gains on Online-Mind2Web and VisualWebArena.

sections.heading: 2.1 Web UI Understanding and Datasets
sections.text: Existing datasets obtain UI annotations either from webpage structure metadata or directly from screenshots. Structure-derived datasets—including WebUI ( Wu et al., 2023 ) , SeeClick ( Cheng et al., 2024 ) , and PixelWeb ( Yang et al., 2025 ) —scale efficiently by leveraging AXTree or DOM information, but their labels depend on heterogeneous HTML, DOM, or accessibility conventions and often require page-specific heuristics to obtain unified semantic types and visually aligned boundaries. Screenshot-based methods such as OmniParser ( Lu et al., 2024 ) and ScreenAI ( Baechler et al., 2024 ) avoid dependence on webpage structure but can suffer from category ambiguity, coordinate offsets, or errors inherited from individual recognition components; high-quality manually annotated datasets ( Nayak et al., 2025 ; Dicu et al., 2025 ) are limited in scale. AtomBlock-WebUI differs from both lines by injecting a predefined semantic taxonomy into webpage HTML before rendering and extracting bounding boxes from the corresponding rendered nodes, providing visually aligned, dual-granularity (block-level and atomic-level) supervision for screenshot-to-TSM rendering.

sections.heading: 2.2 GUI World Models and State Representations
sections.text: GUI world models support either inference-time action selection ( Mei et al., 2026 ; Gu et al., 2025 ) or training-trajectory synthesis ( Xiao et al., 2026 ; Zuo et al., 2026 ) . Across both settings, the choice of state representation fundamentally determines which interface information can be predicted, compared, and used for action selection (Figure 1 ). Existing state spaces include: (1) free-form change descriptions ( Chae et al., 2025 ; Gu et al., 2025 ; Shen et al., 2026a ) , which are compact but lack explicit spatial layouts and hierarchical structure; (2) structured text or AXTree representations ( Cao et al., 2026b ; Zuo et al., 2026 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ) , which preserve partial structure but do not consistently expose element locations, visually grounded types, and control states in a unified form; (3) executable HTML code ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Koh et al., 2026 ) , which can retain page structure but whose rendered outputs may deviate from the target layout or content; and (4) future images ( Guan et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) , which retain rich visual information but incur high generation cost and are unreliable for fine-grained text and small elements. These representations typically trade off spatial and hierarchical fidelity against prediction cost and visual grounding. TSM targets this gap by representing visible UI states as typed, spatially explicit, hierarchically organized elements with control states and visual semantics, remaining efficient for action-conditioned prediction and downstream candidate-action comparison. AtomBlock-WebUI provides visually aligned supervision for rendering screenshots into this state space, while MKD2World models action-conditioned transitions within it for Web-agent reasoning. Detailed discussion refer to Appendix D .

sections.heading: Typed Spatial Markdown Definition.
sections.text: We represent a TSM state as M t = ( ℬ t , ℰ t , ρ t ) M_{t}=(\mathcal{B}_{t},\mathcal{E}_{t},\rho_{t}) , where ℬ t \mathcal{B}_{t} and ℰ t \mathcal{E}_{t} are the sets of block-level and atomic-level elements, respectively, and ρ t \rho_{t} denotes the hierarchical membership relations among UI elements. We define 6 block-level types and 8 atomic-level types. A block-level element is written as b = ( τ b , p ) b=(\tau^{b},p) , and an atomic-level element as e = ( u , c , τ e , p ) e=(u,c,\tau^{e},p) . Here, u u denotes the optional control state, c c denotes visible text or visual semantics, and τ \tau denotes the semantic type. The bounding box is defined as p = ( x , y , w , h ) p=(x,y,w,h) , representing the center coordinates, width, and height of a UI element, with values normalized to [ 0,999 ] [0,999] . More details are provided in Appendix E . Figure 2: Comparison of AtomBlock-WebUI’s direct annotation vs. conventional inference-based annotation. (a) AtomBlock-WebUI injects yolo-* labels into HTML, renders in Chromium, and reads boxes straight from those DOM nodes. (b) Inference-based annotation (DOM rules or VLMs) on heterogeneous pages yields misaligned boxes.

sections.heading: AtomBlock-WebUI Construction.
sections.text: As shown in Figure 2 , we first deduplicate the webpage screenshots in Multimodal-Mind2Web ( Zheng et al., 2024 ) using fingerprint-based filtering. We then use the screenshots as layout reference and employ Qwen3.6-Plus to generate HTML with explicit yolo-* labels and image descriptions. We retrieve semantically matched images from the CC3M ( Sharma et al., 2018 ) image–text dataset and inject the image into HTML. Finally, we use Playwright to drive Chromium and render full-page screenshots. The annotation program directly retrieves the yolo-* DOM nodes to obtain bounding boxes. sections.heading: Screenshot-to-TSM Renderer.
sections.text: Given a webpage screenshot, the renderer converts it into TSM using a YOLO26 ( Jocher et al., 2026 ) UI detector trained on AtomBlock-WebUI, PP-OCRv6 ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and Qwen3.5-0.8B. It first uses the UI detector to identify element types and coordinates and PP-OCRv6 to recognize text, then binds the recognized text to the corresponding elements. Some regions are cropped and passed to Qwen3.5-0.8B for visual semantics. Finally, the renderer constructs a UI Element Tree with containment relationships and sorts the elements according to their spatial relationships to obtain the TSM representation. Details are in Appendix E.2 . Figure 4: Overview of MKD2World. (a) The TSM renderer combines text, type-box, and visual semantics to convert screenshots into TSM. (b) MKD2World learns current-state reconstruction and next-state prediction in two stages, followed by TSM-aware web agent training. (c) A confident single candidate is executed directly; otherwise, MKD2World predicts next states, and the web agent turns them into digests for action selection. (d) MKD2World rollout path for one candidate.

sections.heading: Dataset Construction.
sections.text: We extract ( I t , a t , I t + 1 ) (I_{t},a_{t},I_{t+1}) from WebChain ( Fan et al., 2026 ) and MolmoWeb-HumanTrajs ( Gupta et al., 2026 ) , and use the renderer to obtain ( I t , a t , I t + 1 , M t , M t + 1 ) (I_{t},a_{t},I_{t+1},M_{t},M_{t+1}) . We then perform quality filtering on the transition pairs and categorize them into exact_noop , near_noop , and changed according to the visual differences between the current and next screenshots. To optimize the MKD2World supervised fine-tuning (SFT) loss, we annotate add and update elements in each transition as focus elements. We use the VLM diagnose failure cases and refine rule-based matching criteria; final focus labels are generated by the deterministic rules. We manually audit a stratified sample across all action types. Labels of whether each transition changed and which elements are in focus ultimately supervise MKD2World learning. Details are in Appendix G .

sections.text: We propose EleF1 to measure the similarity between the TSM representations of two interfaces. Let 𝒫 \mathcal{P} and 𝒢 \mathcal{G} denote the element sets parsed from the predicted and ground-truth TSM. For an element pair ( p i , g j ) (p_{i},g_{j}) , we define the matching score as s i ​ j = s sem ​ ( p i , g j ) ⋅ s type ​ ( p i , g j ) ⋅ s spa ​ ( p i , g j ) . \displaystyle s_{ij}=s_{\mathrm{sem}}(p_{i},g_{j})\cdot s_{\mathrm{type}}(p_{i},g_{j})\cdot s_{\mathrm{spa}}(p_{i},g_{j}). (6) Here, s sem s_{\mathrm{sem}} measures the semantic similarity of element content, s type s_{\mathrm{type}} measures element-type compatibility, and s spa s_{\mathrm{spa}} measures spatial consistency by jointly considering bounding-box overlap and center distance. sections.heading: 3.4 World Model Enhanced Web Agent
sections.text: At each decision step, the web agent first generates a candidate action set 𝒜 t = { ( a k , i k ) } k = 1 K \mathcal{A}_{t}=\{(a_{k},i_{k})\}_{k=1}^{K} , where a k a_{k} is a candidate action and i k i_{k} is its intent. The web agent decides whether to invoke the world model based on its confidence. For each candidate action, MKD2World takes the current screenshot I t I_{t} and the candidate action a k a_{k} as input and predicts the interface state S ^ k \hat{S}_{k} . The web agent compresses each prediction into a structured digest d k = Digest ⁡ ( I t , a k , i k , S ^ k ) d_{k}=\operatorname{Digest}(I_{t},a_{k},i_{k},\hat{S}_{k}) , which includes a textual description of the main changes, their consistency with the action intent, their effectiveness in advancing the task, and evidence from S ^ k \hat{S}_{k} . Finally, the web agent aggregates all digests d k d_{k} and selects the best action to execute. In addition, we conduct TSM-aware training for the web agent, training it to describe interface states in TSM and improve interaction ability with MKD2World.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: In this section, we first evaluate the annotation quality of AtomBlock-WebUI. We then assess the prediction accuracy of MKD2World. Finally, we enhance web agents with MKD2World and evaluate their performance on GUI tasks.

sections.heading: Comparison Datasets.
sections.text: We compare AtomBlock-WebUI with four desktop Web UI annotation datasets: ScreenParse-v2, WebUI-CHI23, WebUI-COCO, and UI-Elements. We first deduplicate each dataset. For ScreenParse-v2 and WebUI-CHI23, we randomly sample 1,000 viewport pages from their training sets. WebUI-COCO and UI-Elements use all 618 and 508 pages. AtomBlock-WebUI uses the same set of 1,000 full webpages and reports two evaluation settings: AtomBlock-Top evaluates only the top 16:9 viewport of each page, while AtomBlock-Full averages the evaluation results over all viewports of the same page. Each dataset uses its native viewport resolution and retains only desktop viewports, predominantly 1920 × 1080 1920\times 1080 .

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: Each dataset is annotated under its own category taxonomy. We use GPT-5.6-Sol with low thinking effort to evaluate annotation quality. Given the original screenshot, the annotated screenshot, and script-computed statistics comprising drawable-box count in the current viewport, distinct-category count, occupied cells in a 4 × 4 4\times 4 grid of annotation centers, and HSV color entropy of the original image, the evaluator scores four dimensions: object validity assesses whether recognizable UI elements appear inside the boxes; boundary alignment assesses whether element boundaries align with the annotation boxes; label semantics assesses whether annotated categories are compatible with the element semantics; page complexity is judged from the original image alone and reflects how richly structured the interface is. We randomly sample 20 pages from each dataset and score them with humans to validate the GPT judge against human ratings. sections.heading: Annotation Quality.
sections.text: AtomBlock-Top leads the VLM judge by 2.53 / 2.26 / 2.69 points on boundary alignment, label semantics, and page complexity, and also ranks top under human evaluation with object validity and the best complexity. AtomBlock-Full stays close, leading human boundary alignment and label semantics, with only a mild drop in complexity on full pages.

sections.heading: Community Adoption.
sections.text: AtomBlock-WebUI is released on Hugging Face and has accrued over 7K downloads; it also ranked Top-5 on the Hugging Face dataset trending leaderboard. These signals suggest that the dataset addresses a clear community need for well-annotated Web UI resources.

sections.heading: Datasets and Metrics.
sections.text: We extract interface transitions from WebChain and MolmoWeb-HumanTrajs. After quality filtering, domain-based splitting, TSM rendering, and focus annotation, we obtain a 100k Current-State reconstruction training set and a 31k Next-State prediction training set. We reserve 500 validation transitions for model selection and result analysis, and evaluate all models on in-domain (ID) and out-of-domain (OOD) test sets. Each test set contains 1,000 transitions across five action categories: click, text/key, scroll, navigation, and other, with 200 transitions per category. We further maintain a balanced website distribution as much as possible (see Appendix G.1 ). For metrics, EleF1 measures the similarity between the predicted TSM and the ground-truth TSM. We report EleF1 for five action categories and use Overall to denote the average value. Format Success measures the ratio of generated TSM outputs that can be successfully parsed.

sections.heading: Model Settings.
sections.text: MKD2World is built on Qwen3.5-9B and trained with the same LoRA configuration in two-stage SFT. Across both stages, we apply LoRA to all 32 language-model layers and to the attention and MLP modules in each of the 27 vision-encoder blocks, with rank r = 32 r=32 , α = 64 \alpha=64 , and dropout 0.05 0.05 . We optimize with AdamW at a learning rate of 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} , use seed 0 0 , cap supervised outputs at 6,000 6{,}000 tokens, and train on A800 GPUs. sections.text: As shown in Table 2 , MKD2World achieves the highest EleF1 on both ID and OOD test sets. Navigation remains the most challenging category for all methods, likely because its target interface can change substantially beyond the visible context of the source page. sections.heading: Datasets and Metrics.
sections.text: We evaluate the effectiveness of MKD2World in improving web agent performance on Online-Mind2Web ( Xue et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2023 ) and VisualWebArena ( Koh et al., 2024 ) . Online-Mind2Web contains 300 real-time website tasks. After removing unavailable tasks and tasks heavily affected by network instability, we select 109 relatively stable tasks as our test set, including 25 Easy, 48 Medium, and 36 Hard tasks (see Appendix H ). The interaction trajectories are reviewed by GPT-5.6-Sol under a unified criterion to determine whether each task is successfully completed. The judge receives the task instruction, the full trajectory of screenshots in temporal order, the action history, the agent’s final answer, and runtime error logs. An early stop by the web agent does not count as success. We set success = 1 \mathrm{success}=1 only when the screenshots and action records show that all task requirements are completed; ambiguous, incomplete evidence, or termination at the 50 50 -step budget yields 0 0 . Additionally, we use 233 tasks from VisualWebArena as a supplementary benchmark to further evaluate the generalization ability of MKD2World. Success on VisualWebArena is determined by the benchmark’s official checkers rather than trajectory quality. After the agent stops, the checkers inspect the final page and the last submitted answer and return a binary score under rules.

sections.heading: Model Settings.
sections.text: We enhance four web agents with MKD2World: Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, Qwen3.5-9B, GUI-Owl-1.5-8B ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , and deepseek-v4.1-flash. We use WMA, WebDreamer, Qwen-AgentWorld, and WebWorld as world model baselines. When comparing different world models, we hold the agent fixed to Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on Online-Mind2Web and to Qwen3.5-9B on VisualWebArena. All web agents follow the same policy: the input is the current screenshot, the action history, and the task goal; the output is only one action type with normalized coordinates. With world-model support, a web agent may emit one or more candidate actions according to its confidence. We set the context length to 32K tokens, the output length to 5K tokens, and thinking effort to medium. We cap each episode at 50 steps and stop after 4 consecutive repeated actions. All world models make predictions under their official prompting strategies. We cap world-model outputs at 6K tokens, disable thinking mode, and set temperature to 0 0 . For MKD2World, we further fine-tune all web agents except DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash for TSM awareness, using a 50K subset of the Current-State reconstruction training set at a learning rate of 2 × 10 − 6 2\times 10^{-6} ; all other settings match those used to train MKD2World for Current-State reconstruction in the previous subsection. We further add a digest step in which the web agent consolidates the MKD2World’s predictions before acting. This adaptation strengthens collaboration between the web agent and MKD2World.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we presented TSM, a complete structured interface state, and constructed viewport-controllable AtomBlock-WebUI with balanced types and precise boxes. We further introduced MKD2World and proposed digest and TSM-awareness to strengthen WebAgent–MKD2World collaboration. Empirically, MKD2World outperforms GPT-5.6-Sol on prediction accuracy and boosts Qwen3.5-35B by + 14.67 % +14.67\% on Online-Mind2Web. Despite the improvements, due to the complexity and frequent updates of web interfaces, MKD2World cannot achieve pixel-level aligned prediction. Our current setting targets static pages; it does not yet perform temporal understanding of audio, video, or animation, nor predict audiovisual changes over the next time interval.

sections.heading: Appendix C AtomBlock-WebUI Construction and Statistics
sections.text: We perform fingerprint-based near-duplicate filtering on screenshots from Multimodal-Mind2Web. Each image is converted to grayscale, resized to 17 × 16 17\times 16 with Lanczos interpolation, and encoded as a 256-bit difference hash (dHash) by comparing adjacent pixels in each row. Screenshots whose hashes have Hamming distance d H ​ ( h i , h j ) = popcount ⁡ ( h i ⊕ h j ) ≤ 5 d_{H}(h_{i},h_{j})=\operatorname{popcount}(h_{i}\oplus h_{j})\leq 5 are connected in a graph; each connected component keeps one randomly selected image. Subsequently, we use the filtered screenshots as layout references and generate HTML with Qwen3.6-Plus. We require the model to cover 8 atomic and 6 block types, inject yolo-* category labels and vary color schemes for visual diversity. Each image node is an tag with a data-caption attribute. We next inject CC3M images into pages. For each node, we encode its data-caption with MiniLM-L6-v2 and retrieve the top-50 candidates via FAISS. We then re-rank by aspect-ratio mismatch with the target region and randomly pick one of the top-5. The chosen image is resized to the node and written back to the HTML. We render pages with Playwright-driven Chromium and collect bounding boxes from nodes tagged with yolo-* labels. We retain the original image-injected HTML, so each page can be re-rendered under different viewports while producing consistent annotations. AtomBlock-WebUI comprises 9,683 full-page screenshots and 1,321,234 type–bounding box annotations, split into 6,906, 1,388, and 1,389 pages for training, validation, and testing. sections.heading: D.1 Web UI Understanding and Datasets
sections.text: Web UI understanding requires identifying visible interface elements together with their semantic types and spatial extents. Existing datasets and methods obtain such annotations primarily from webpage structure metadata or from visual recognition. 1. Structure-derived annotations. WebUI ( Wu et al., 2023 ) constructs UI datasets through rule-based parsing of the AXTree, extracting UI elements and their corresponding bounding boxes. SeeClick ( Cheng et al., 2024 ) and MultiUI ( Liu et al., 2024 ) similarly derive annotations from webpage structural metadata, but are commonly used for task-oriented grounding rather than dense full-page annotation of all visible UI elements. WebCode2M ( Gui et al., 2025 ) collects real webpage screenshots and DOM-node information to annotate webpage structures, whereas PixelWeb ( Yang et al., 2025 ) obtains visible element boundaries through DOM information and pixel-level rendering, with its public release including substantial mobile-web data. These approaches benefit from available webpage metadata, but their labels depend on heterogeneous HTML, DOM, or accessibility structures; obtaining a unified semantic taxonomy and visually aligned element boundaries therefore often requires page-specific heuristics. 2. Screenshot-based UI understanding. Visual methods instead infer UI elements directly from screenshots. OmniParser ( Lu et al., 2024 ) detects interactive regions but covers a limited set of categories and can be sensitive to model parameters. ScreenAI ( Baechler et al., 2024 ) combines OCR, UI detectors, and image captioning models to generate large-scale annotations, whose quality may inherit errors from individual recognition components. ScreenParse ( Gurbuz et al., 2026 ) uses VLMs for UI-element category prediction and quality filtering. UICVD ( Nayak et al., 2025 ) and GenGUI ( Dicu et al., 2025 ) rely on manual annotation and provide high-quality labels, but at limited scale. While screenshot-based approaches avoid dependence on webpage structure, they may still suffer from category ambiguity and coordinate offsets. AtomBlock-WebUI differs from both lines of work by injecting a predefined semantic taxonomy into webpage HTML before rendering and extracting bounding boxes from the corresponding rendered nodes. It thereby provides visually aligned, dual-granularity annotations over both block-level and atomic-level elements. Rather than targeting only task-relevant grounding or generic UI detection, it is designed to supervise screenshot-to-structured-state rendering for TSM construction.

sections.heading: D.2 GUI World Models and State Representations
sections.text: GUI world models follow two broad paradigms. For inference-time decision enhancement, a world model predicts the next interface state conditioned on each candidate action, and a value model scores the predictions to select the best action ( Mei et al., 2026 ; Gu et al., 2025 ) . For training data synthesis, agents interact with world models over multiple steps to produce interaction trajectories that are then used for agent training ( Xiao et al., 2026 ; Fang et al., 2025 ; Zuo et al., 2026 ) . Across both settings, the choice of state representation fundamentally determines which interface information can be predicted, compared, and used for action selection. Figure 1 summarizes the central trade-off among representative GUI state representations: preserving rich, structured interface information while avoiding the cost and instability of pixel-level reconstruction. 1. Free-form textual change descriptions. WMA ( Chae et al., 2025 ) , WebDreamer ( Gu et al., 2025 ) , and WAC ( Shen et al., 2026a ) describe post-action interface changes as free-form natural-language text. This representation is compact and easy for language models to generate, but typically does not explicitly encode element-level spatial layouts, does not provide a structured, comparable state, and makes it difficult to evaluate prediction accuracy or directly compare candidate outcomes. 2. Structured textual and accessibility representations. MobileDreamer ( Cao et al., 2026b ) uses structured text to describe mobile Web interfaces, capturing some hierarchical layout but supporting only a limited set of element types and omitting many interactive elements and block-level structures. Qwen-AgentWorld ( Zuo et al., 2026 ) and WebWorld ( Xiao et al., 2026 ) predict AXTree representations in Web environments, and more broadly, AXTree and DOM have been widely adopted as structured observations for GUI agents. However, these representations do not consistently expose explicit element locations or visually grounded semantics in a form suitable for state comparison, hindering direct use for pixel-aligned state prediction and candidate-action evaluation. 3. Code and image state representations. Code2World ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) and gWorld ( Koh et al., 2026 ) predict future states as HTML code that is subsequently rendered into images; however, the rendered pages often lack realistic visual assets and can diverge from real webpage layouts. CUWM ( Guan et al., 2026 ) predicts future states directly as interface images, but incurs high generation cost and tends to produce distorted or blurry small text. ViMo ( Luo et al., 2025 ) masks text regions, predicts a text-free image, and uses an LLM to infill text, but this decoupled generation lacks tight semantic grounding in spatial elements and can produce inaccurate fine-grained content. Prior work has studied UI understanding datasets, GUI element grounding, and action-conditioned world modeling, but these lines have not jointly provided a state space that is spatially explicit, hierarchically structured, and efficient to predict. TSM fills this gap by serializing complete UI states into typed spatial elements. AtomBlock-WebUI supplies aligned supervision for rendering screenshots into this state space, and MKD2World models action-conditioned transitions within it.

sections.heading: E.2 TSM Renderer Details
sections.text: The screenshot renderer converts a webpage screenshot into a TSM state using a YOLO26 detector trained on AtomBlock-WebUI, PP-OCRv6, and Qwen3.5-0.8B. A child block is contained in a parent if its center lies inside the parent and the parent covers more than 85% of its area. The block priorities are 0 for Navigation , Sidebar , and Footer , 1 for Form and Table , and 2 for Section (lower is high priority). So generic Section do not override function-specific blocks. For each atomic element, we first take blocks that contain its center; otherwise those covering at least 50% of its area. Among candidates, we keep the smallest block with the highest priority; unmatched elements stay at the TSM top level. Qwen3.5-0.8B describes images and icons, and judges states of checkboxes, radios, and selects. For checkboxes and radios, we enlarge the crop to capture the same line. For selects, we extend the crop downward and treat the dropdown as open if options appear.

sections.heading: G.2 Focus Annotation
sections.text: Focus annotations exist only for changed transitions. Given states S t S_{t} and S t + 1 S_{t+1} , we mark add and update elements in S t + 1 S_{t+1} and record their spans to compute the Base–Focus Element Loss. Directly comparing S t S_{t} and S t + 1 S_{t+1} may confuse rendering noise or minor positional shifts with actual changes. We therefore match elements between the two TSM states. For each element, we parse content, type, state, and bbox, and record its span in the TSM string. For text-input actions, we first match the element at the action location. If multiple nearby elements share a similar shift, we keep them matched. We then match elements with aligned semantics and bboxes, then those with aligned semantics but shifted bboxes. Unmatched elements are labeled add only if they pass a reliability filter. A matched element is update if any of content, state, or bbox changes reliably.

sections.heading: I.7 Online-Mind2Web Trajectory Judgment
sections.text: ⬇ # Independent Online - Mind2Web trajectory judgment You are an independent strict judge . Inspect this one trajectory only . The attached screenshots are ordered chronologically and correspond exactly to : ["0000. png ", "0001. png ", "..."] Use the screenshots and action log as evidence . The agent ’ s final answer and ‘ agent_finish ‘ status are untrusted claims , not proof of success . ## Success rule - Return success =1 only when the visual / action evidence proves every material requirement in the task instruction was completed . - For cart / form / state - changing tasks , require evidence of the resulting state ; reaching a relevant page or merely attempting the last action is insufficient . - For comparison or information tasks , require that the requested information was actually reached and visible / readable enough to answer the instruction . - If evidence is ambiguous , incomplete , contradicted , or ends at max steps , use 0. - Do not award success just because an action has action_status = SUCCESS ; that only means browser execution returned , not that the benchmark goal was achieved . ## Technical - failure rule - environment_technical_failure = true only for objective environment failures such as DNS / network / browser failure , persistent server error , inaccessible page , or an external blocking challenge that prevents evaluation . - model_technical_failure = true only for model / pipeline failures such as empty or malformed model output , generation / API failure , action parse failure , or an execution_error attributable to the agent pipeline . - Ordinary bad planning , wrong clicks , repetition , premature finish , and max_steps are task failures but are NOT model technical failures . - A successful task may still have a transient technical failure only if the trajectory clearly recovered and ultimately proves completion . ## Evidence payload { " task_id ": "< task_id >", " task_instruction ": "< task instruction >", " agent_final_answer ": "< agent final answer >", " reference_length ": "< reference length >", " run_metadata ": {}, " action_history ": [], " runtime_diagnostics ": { " raw_step_count ": 0, " execution_errors ": [] } } ## Output contract Return exactly one JSON object and nothing else : { " task_id ": "< task_id >", " success ": 0, " reason ": " one concise evidence - based sentence ", " key_evidence_steps ": [0], " key_evidence_screenshots ": ["0000. png "], " environment_technical_failure ": false , " model_technical_failure ": false , " technical_failure_type ": " none ", " technical_failure_reason ": "" } The success value must be integer 0 or 1. sections.heading: I.8 Web UI Datasets’ Annotation Judgment
sections.text: ⬇ TASK CONTRACT Evaluate exactly one desktop Web UI screenshot sample . Return four independent quality scores from 0 to 100. Judge only the evidence in this call . Do not identify or guess the dataset , collection method , author , website , or benchmark . IMAGE ROLES Image A is the unannotated screenshot . Use Image A only for page_complexity . Image B is the same screenshot with thin black - and - white annotation outlines and small numeric box identifiers . SCORING RUBRIC 1. annotation_object_validity Definition : The proportion of evaluable annotations that correspond to a visually recognizable UI element or meaningful UI region . Atomic controls , text , images , groups , containers , navigation regions , content regions , and other structural blocks can be valid targets . Anchors : - 0: No usable annotation corresponds to a recognizable intended target , or annotation_state fixes this score at zero . - 25: Only a small minority of annotations have recognizable intended targets ; empty or background - only boxes dominate . - 50: Recognizable and unrecognizable intended targets are roughly balanced . - 75: Most annotations have recognizable intended targets , with a noticeable minority of empty , background - only , or unusable annotations . - 100: Essentially every evaluable annotation has a clearly recognizable intended target and source - level machine issues are absent or negligible . 2. boundary_alignment Definition : How well assessable original sides represent reasonable boundaries for recognizable target semantics . Atomic visual elements should have visually tight or appropriate interaction boundaries . Text or CSS - content labels may use content - oriented boxes . Structural regions may use semantic grouping boundaries . Anchors : - 0: Assessable sides are almost entirely unrelated to , or severely displaced from , their recognizable targets . - 25: Major displacement , excessive extent , or severe clipping affects most assessable original sides . - 50: Assessable original sides show a roughly even mix of reasonable and materially inaccurate placement . - 75: Most assessable original sides reasonably delimit their targets , with a noticeable minority that are loose , shifted , clipped , or undersized . - 100: Essentially all assessable sides closely match reasonable atomic , interaction , content , or structural boundaries for their targets . 3. label_semantic_reasonableness Definition : Whether each valid , recognizable target ’ s complete provided label set is semantically compatible with that target under the supplied ‘ classes ‘ table . Broad functional , visual , accessibility - role , atomic , and structural labels can all be reasonable . Compatible multi - label descriptions are valid . Anchors : - 0: Equal - weight semantic contributions are essentially all zero ; supplied labels are incompatible with their visible targets . - 25: Equal - weight semantic contributions average near one quarter ; most annotations have incompatible or largely incompatible label sets . - 50: Equal - weight semantic contributions average near one half , reflecting a roughly balanced mixture of compatible and incompatible labels within annotations . - 75: Equal - weight semantic contributions average near three quarters ; most annotations have fully or mostly compatible label sets , with a noticeable minority of mismatches . - 100: Equal - weight semantic contributions are essentially all one ; every supplied label is compatible with its visible target and supplied ontology . 4. page_complexity Definition : The amount , diversity , and depth of visible UI structure in Image A . Consider layout hierarchy , visible regions , component variety , information density , spatial relationships , typography , imagery , color relationships , and interaction affordances together . Anchors : - 0: Almost blank or visually empty , with essentially no discernible page structure or content . - 25: A sparse page with one simple region , few visible component types , and little hierarchy or information . - 50: A moderately structured page with several regions or component types and ordinary information density . - 75: Many visible regions and component types , with substantial hierarchy or dense spatial relationships . - 100: Exceptionally many diverse UI regions and components with very deep or dense visible relationships , regardless of presentation quality . OUTPUT CONTRACT Return exactly one JSON object and nothing else : { " sample_id ": "< sample_id >", " annotation_object_validity ": 0, " boundary_alignment ": 0, " label_semantic_reasonableness ": 0, " page_complexity ": 0 } Each score is an integer from 0 to 100. Copy sample_id from the supplied sample .

Abstract Graphical user interface (GUI) agents can improve decision-making with world-model foresight, provided that predicted states accurately reflect post-action interfaces. Existing state representations fail to jointly capture interface layout, UI semantics, and explicit locations. We introduce Typed Spatial Markdown (TSM) , a Markdown-style textual state representation for desktop web interfaces. TSM serializes block-level and atomic-level UI elements according to their spatial relationships, jointly encoding their types, visual semantics, explicit locations, optional control states, and hierarchical membership. To train a screenshot-to-TSM renderer, we construct AtomBlock-WebUI , a dataset with precise annotations at both granularities. By injecting element-type labels into HTML and directly extracting bounding boxes after rendering, we avoid annotation errors caused by post-hoc inference from webpage structures. Building on TSM, we propose MKD2World , a desktop web world model trained in two stages for current-state description and action-conditioned next-state prediction. During inference, the web agent queries MKD2World as needed and performs a “digest” step, in which it interprets each predicted state and extracts task-relevant evidence for selecting the best action. Experiments show that MKD2World-9B achieves an EleF1 score of 26.50 on the out-of-domain test set, outperforming GPT-5.6-Sol(14.98) by 11.52 points. Across Online-Mind2Web tasks, MKD2World-9B improves the success rate of the Qwen3.5-35B web agent from 22.94% to 37.61%, achieving competitive performance among leading open-source GUI world models. Code is available at https://github.com/OmniAI-Lab-CUHKSZ/MKD2World . 1 Introduction With the development of vision-language models (VLMs), graphical user interface (GUI) agents have become capable of completing interactive tasks in real-world scenarios ( Cao et al., 2026a ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) . At each decision step, an agent generates an executable action based on the task objective, current interface, and historical information. However, without sufficient understanding of webpage dynamics—including the functions of user interface (UI) controls and the logic of interface transitions—it may generate ineffective actions that increase interaction costs or cause irreversible errors, such as accidentally deleting important data or leaking private information ( Shen et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Action-conditioned world models offer a promising way to anticipate future interface states before execution, helping agents assess whether candidate actions advance the task while reducing risky real interactions ( Mei et al., 2026 ; Gu et al., 2025 ) . The usefulness of such foresight depends on what state a world model predicts . Figure 1 compares representative GUI state representations and highlights the desired trade-off: preserving a complete, structured interface state without incurring the cost of pixel-level reconstruction. We argue that, to distinguish the consequences of candidate actions, a predicted state should preserve a complete yet structured account of the post-action interface, including both the elements that change and the surrounding context needed to interpret those changes—their semantics, locations, control states, and structural relations. At the same time, it should avoid the cost and instability of reconstructing every visual detail of a webpage. Existing GUI world models represent states as free-form descriptions of interface changes, structured interface representations such as the Accessibility Tree (AXTree) and Document Object Model (DOM) ( Zuo et al., 2026 ) , HTML rendered into webpages ( Koh et al., 2026 ) , or images generated directly by image generation models ( Guan et al., 2026 ) . Free-form text concisely conveys major changes but loses layout structure and substantial information from the next interface. Common AXTree and DOM serializations preserve parts of the interface structure, yet often omit explicit element locations and have incomplete visual semantics ( Wu et al., 2023 ) . Other structured textual representations retain some layout and locations, but support limited element types and omit UI control states, complete visual semantics, or interface block structure ( Cao et al., 2026b ) . HTML-rendered images may omit actual images or deviate from the real layout, whereas pure image-generation approaches are costly and often distort fine-grained text ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) . Thus, these representations do not adequately balance preserving a complete, structured interface state with avoiding the burden of full visual reconstruction. This limits the completeness of the interface information available to a world model and, in turn, to downstream agent reasoning. To address this bottleneck, we introduce Typed Spatial Markdown (TSM) , a structured and spatially grounded state representation for desktop Web interfaces. TSM organizes rendered Web UIs into block-level and atomic-level elements according to their spatial relationships. Each entry encodes its type, visual semantics, bounding box, optional control state, and hierarchical membership, jointly capturing what an element is, where it appears, what it conveys, and how it is organized. Markdown provides a readable hierarchical serialization of this structured state. By retaining the interface information needed to compare action-induced changes without reconstructing the full pixel-level interface, TSM provides a compact and directly comparable state space for action-conditioned world modeling and downstream agent reasoning. Learning this state space from screenshots requires reliable UI element types and locations. Existing desktop Web UI datasets often extract them from the DOM or AXTree through rule-based parsing ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Gurbuz et al., 2026 ) . However, HTML structures are highly heterogeneous across webpages: tags and class names are typically tied to page styling and interactions, while role attributes are often incomplete, making unified and reliable semantic annotations difficult to obtain ( Gou et al., 2025 ) . Post-hoc DOM parsing can therefore assign types to visually invisible elements or yield misaligned bounding boxes; visual models may likewise localize elements away from their actual positions ( Fu et al., 2026 ) . To reduce ambiguities introduced by such post-hoc semantic inference, we construct AtomBlock-WebUI . A VLM generates HTML with reference to real webpage layouts and explicitly injects predefined UI element types. After rendering, we directly extract the coordinates of the corresponding typed DOM nodes. This pipeline provides visually aligned type and location supervision for the dual-granularity UI detector in our TSM renderer. Building on TSM and AtomBlock-WebUI, we introduce MKD2World , an action-conditioned desktop Web world model that predicts future TSM states from screenshots and candidate actions. MKD2World first learns to reconstruct the current interface in the TSM state space, and then learns action-conditioned state transitions with transition-aware objectives that emphasize the elements changed by an action. At inference time, it simulates a next TSM state for each candidate action. We further train the GUI agent to understand TSM and design a digest-based inference strategy, through which the agent interprets predicted typed, spatial, and stateful changes to select the action that best advances the user objective. The main contributions of this work are as follows: • Typed Spatial Markdown (TSM). We propose TSM, a structured and spatially grounded Web UI state representation that encodes UI semantics, explicit spatial information, control states, and hierarchical structures, together with a screenshot-to-TSM renderer. • AtomBlock-WebUI Dataset. We construct a 9.7k-scale desktop Web UI annotation dataset using a pre-injected automated annotation pipeline, providing element types and bounding boxes for both block-level and atomic-level UI elements to train the dual-granularity UI detector in the screenshot-to-TSM renderer. • MKD2World: A TSM World Model for Web Agents. We propose MKD2World, an action-conditioned desktop Web world model that predicts future TSM states from screenshots and candidate actions. MKD2World uses a two-stage training scheme with transition-aware objectives, and supports uncertainty-triggered, digest-based action selection by TSM-aware Web agents. • Comprehensive Evaluation and Online Validation. We propose EleF1 to evaluate TSM prediction accuracy, and demonstrate strong out-of-domain prediction and consistent decision-making gains on Online-Mind2Web and VisualWebArena. 2 Related Work 2.1 Web UI Understanding and Datasets Existing datasets obtain UI annotations either from webpage structure metadata or directly from screenshots. Structure-derived datasets—including WebUI ( Wu et al., 2023 ) , SeeClick ( Cheng et al., 2024 ) , and PixelWeb ( Yang et al., 2025 ) —scale efficiently by leveraging AXTree or DOM information, but their labels depend on heterogeneous HTML, DOM, or accessibility conventions and often require page-specific heuristics to obtain unified semantic types and visually aligned boundaries. Screenshot-based methods such as OmniParser ( Lu et al., 2024 ) and ScreenAI ( Baechler et al., 2024 ) avoid dependence on webpage structure but can suffer from category ambiguity, coordinate offsets, or errors inherited from individual recognition components; high-quality manually annotated datasets ( Nayak et al., 2025 ; Dicu et al., 2025 ) are limited in scale. AtomBlock-WebUI differs from both lines by injecting a predefined semantic taxonomy into webpage HTML before rendering and extracting bounding boxes from the corresponding rendered nodes, providing visually aligned, dual-granularity (block-level and atomic-level) supervision for screenshot-to-TSM rendering. 2.2 GUI World Models and State Representations GUI world models support either inference-time action selection ( Mei et al., 2026 ; Gu et al., 2025 ) or training-trajectory synthesis ( Xiao et al., 2026 ; Zuo et al., 2026 ) . Across both settings, the choice of state representation fundamentally determines which interface information can be predicted, compared, and used for action selection (Figure 1 ). Existing state spaces include: (1) free-form change descriptions ( Chae et al., 2025 ; Gu et al., 2025 ; Shen et al., 2026a ) , which are compact but lack explicit spatial layouts and hierarchical structure; (2) structured text or AXTree representations ( Cao et al., 2026b ; Zuo et al., 2026 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ) , which preserve partial structure but do not consistently expose element locations, visually grounded types, and control states in a unified form; (3) executable HTML code ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Koh et al., 2026 ) , which can retain page structure but whose rendered outputs may deviate from the target layout or content; and (4) future images ( Guan et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) , which retain rich visual information but incur high generation cost and are unreliable for fine-grained text and small elements. These representations typically trade off spatial and hierarchical fidelity against prediction cost and visual grounding. TSM targets this gap by representing visible UI states as typed, spatially explicit, hierarchically organized elements with control states and visual semantics, remaining efficient for action-conditioned prediction and downstream candidate-action comparison. AtomBlock-WebUI provides visually aligned supervision for rendering screenshots into this state space, while MKD2World models action-conditioned transitions within it for Web-agent reasoning. We evaluate the effectiveness of MKD2World in improving web agent performance on Online-Mind2Web ( Xue et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2023 ) and VisualWebArena ( Koh et al., 2024 ) . Online-Mind2Web contains 300 real-time website tasks. After removing unavailable tasks and tasks heavily affected by network instability, we select 109 relatively stable tasks as our test set, including 25 Easy, 48 Medium, and 36 Hard tasks (see Appendix H ). The interaction trajectories are reviewed by GPT-5.6-Sol under a unified criterion to determine whether each task is successfully completed. The judge receives the task instruction, the full trajectory of screenshots in temporal order, the action history, the agent’s final answer, and runtime error logs. An early stop by the web agent does not count as success. Appendix C AtomBlock-WebUI Construction and Statistics We perform fingerprint-based near-duplicate filtering on screenshots from Multimodal-Mind2Web. Each image is converted to grayscale, resized to 17 × 16 17\times 16 with Lanczos interpolation, and encoded as a 256-bit difference hash (dHash) by comparing adjacent pixels in each row. Screenshots whose hashes have Hamming distance d H ​ ( h i , h j ) = popcount ⁡ ( h i ⊕ h j ) ≤ 5 d_{H}(h_{i},h_{j})=\operatorname{popcount}(h_{i}\oplus h_{j})\leq 5 are connected in a graph; each connected component keeps one randomly selected image. Subsequently, we use the filtered screenshots as layout references and generate HTML with Qwen3.6-Plus. We require the model to cover 8 atomic and 6 block types, inject yolo-* category labels and vary color schemes for visual diversity. Each image node is an <img> tag with a data-caption attribute. We next inject CC3M images into pages. For each <img> node, we encode its data-caption with MiniLM-L6-v2 and retrieve the top-50 candidates via FAISS. We then re-rank by aspect-ratio mismatch with the target region and randomly pick one of the top-5. The chosen image is resized to the node and written back to the HTML. We render pages with Playwright-driven Chromium and collect bounding boxes from nodes tagged with yolo-* labels. We retain the original image-injected HTML, so each page can be re-rendered under different viewports while producing consistent annotations. AtomBlock-WebUI comprises 9,683 full-page screenshots and 1,321,234 type–bounding box annotations, split into 6,906, 1,388, and 1,389 pages for training, validation, and testing. Appendix D Related Work D.1 Web UI Understanding and Datasets Web UI understanding requires identifying visible interface elements together with their semantic types and spatial extents. Existing datasets and methods obtain such annotations primarily from webpage structure metadata or from visual recognition. 1. Structure-derived annotations. WebUI ( Wu et al., 2023 ) constructs UI datasets through rule-based parsing of the AXTree, extracting UI elements and their corresponding bounding boxes. SeeClick ( Cheng et al., 2024 ) and MultiUI ( Liu et al., 2024 ) similarly derive annotations from webpage structural metadata, but are commonly used for task-oriented grounding rather than dense full-page annotation of all visible UI elements. WebCode2M ( Gui et al., 2025 ) collects real webpage screenshots and DOM-node information to annotate webpage structures, whereas PixelWeb ( Yang et al., 2025 ) obtains visible element boundaries through DOM information and pixel-level rendering, with its public release including substantial mobile-web data. These approaches benefit from available webpage metadata, but their labels depend on heterogeneous HTML, DOM, or accessibility structures; obtaining a unified semantic taxonomy and visually aligned element boundaries therefore often requires page-specific heuristics. 2. Screenshot-based UI understanding. Visual methods instead infer UI elements directly from screenshots. OmniParser ( Lu et al., 2024 ) detects interactive regions but covers a limited set of categories and can be sensitive to model parameters. ScreenAI ( Baechler et al., 2024 ) combines OCR, UI detectors, and image captioning models to generate large-scale annotations, whose quality may inherit errors from individual recognition components. ScreenParse ( Gurbuz et al., 2026 ) uses VLMs for UI-element category prediction and quality filtering. UICVD ( Nayak et al., 2025 ) and GenGUI ( Dicu et al., 2025 ) rely on manual annotation and provide high-quality labels, but at limited scale. While screenshot-based approaches avoid dependence on webpage structure, they may still suffer from category ambiguity and coordinate offsets. AtomBlock-WebUI differs from both lines of work by injecting a predefined semantic taxonomy into webpage HTML before rendering and extracting bounding boxes from the corresponding rendered nodes. It thereby provides visually aligned, dual-granularity annotations over both block-level and atomic-level elements. Rather than targeting only task-relevant grounding or generic UI detection, it is designed to supervise screenshot-to-structured-state rendering for TSM construction. D.2 GUI World Models and State Representations GUI world models follow two broad paradigms. For inference-time decision enhancement, a world model predicts the next interface state conditioned on each candidate action, and a value model scores the predictions to select the best action ( Mei et al., 2026 ; Gu et al., 2025 ) . For training data synthesis, agents interact with world models over multiple steps to produce interaction trajectories that are then used for agent training ( Xiao et al., 2026 ; Fang et al., 2025 ; Zuo et al., 2026 ) . Across both settings, the choice of state representation fundamentally determines which interface information can be predicted, compared, and used for action selection. Figure 1 summarizes the central trade-off among representative GUI state representations: preserving rich, structured interface information while avoiding the cost and instability of pixel-level reconstruction. 1. Free-form textual change descriptions. WMA ( Chae et al., 2025 ) , WebDreamer ( Gu et al., 2025 ) , and WAC ( Shen et al., 2026a ) describe post-action interface changes as free-form natural-language text. This representation is compact and easy for language models to generate, but typically does not explicitly encode element-level spatial layouts, does not provide a structured, comparable state, and makes it difficult to evaluate prediction accuracy or directly compare candidate outcomes. 2. Structured textual and accessibility representations. MobileDreamer ( Cao et al., 2026b ) uses structured text to describe mobile Web interfaces, capturing some hierarchical layout but supporting only a limited set of element types and omitting many interactive elements and block-level structures. Qwen-AgentWorld ( Zuo et al., 2026 ) and WebWorld ( Xiao et al., 2026 ) predict AXTree representations in Web environments, and more broadly, AXTree and DOM have been widely adopted as structured observations for GUI agents. However, these representations do not consistently expose explicit element locations or visually grounded semantics in a form suitable for state comparison, hindering direct use for pixel-aligned state prediction and candidate-action evaluation. 3. Code and image state representations. Code2World ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) and gWorld ( Koh et al., 2026 ) predict future states as HTML code that is subsequently rendered into images; however, the rendered pages often lack realistic visual assets and can diverge from real webpage layouts. CUWM ( Guan et al., 2026 ) predicts future states directly as interface images, but incurs high generation cost and tends to produce distorted or blurry small text. ViMo ( Luo et al., 2025 ) masks text regions, predicts a text-free image, and uses an LLM to infill text, but this decoupled generation lacks tight semantic grounding in spatial elements and can produce inaccurate fine-grained content. Prior work has studied UI understanding datasets, GUI element grounding, and action-conditioned world modeling, but these lines have not jointly provided a state space that is spatially explicit, hierarchically structured, and efficient to predict. TSM fills this gap by serializing complete UI states into typed spatial elements. AtomBlock-WebUI supplies aligned supervision for rendering screenshots into this state space, and MKD2World models action-conditioned transitions within it.
